title: WHY GIDEON WAS HIDING BEFORE GOD CALLED HIM
paragraphs: WHY GIDEON WAS HIDING BEFORE GOD CALLED HIM
The sound of wheat hitting stone should have been ordinary.
It should have echoed across an open field beneath the hot Midianite sun. It should have been a farmer's sound. A provider's sound. A free man's sound.
Instead, it was the sound of fear.
Hidden beneath the earth, inside a winepress never designed for grain, a young man worked in secret.
His eyes constantly scanned for danger.
Every movement carried the possibility of loss.
This was not how God intended Israel to live.
And this was not how Gideon imagined his story would unfold.
Yet before God called him a mighty warrior, before armies would follow his command, before miracles would unfold beneath the night sky, Gideon was hiding.
Many believers know the ending of Gideon's story.
And fewer still recognize themselves inside it.
Israel had abandoned covenant faithfulness and turned toward idols. As a result, God allowed Midian to oppress the nation.
Scripture says the Midianites arrived "like locusts in number" (Judges 6:5). They stripped the land bare, consumed harvests, destroyed livelihoods, and left God's people desperate.
The Hebrew text paints a picture of total devastation.
Entire communities learned to survive by remaining unseen.
This is the world Gideon inherited.
A generation that forgot what freedom felt like.
Then comes one of the most astonishing moments in Scripture.
"The angel of the LORD came and sat under the oak in Ophrah."
"The LORD is with you, mighty warrior."
The phrase גִּבּוֹר הֶחָיִל (gibbor he-chayil) means far more than a strong fighter.
A person of extraordinary capability and courage.
But Gideon was none of those things—at least not visibly.
Why would God call a hiding man a mighty warrior?
Because God was speaking to who Gideon would become through grace rather than who he appeared to be through fear.
This is one of the most beautiful themes in all Scripture.
God often introduces Himself to people through their future identity rather than their present condition.
And Gideon becomes a mighty warrior before he ever acts like one.
Many people assume Gideon was hiding because he lacked courage.
Years of oppression had taught him survival.
When fear becomes normal, hiding begins to feel wise.
Some hide behind carefully constructed versions of themselves.
Others hide wounds they have never spoken aloud.
"If the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us?"
This is a wounded believer trying to reconcile God's promises with his experience.
Perhaps you have prayed the same question.
If God is with me, why did the marriage fail?
Why did the prayers seem unanswered?
Why did life become so heavy?
Gideon is asking what countless believers have asked through tears.
Where is God when life falls apart?
God does not condemn the question.
God sees faith waiting to awaken.
The Gospel follows this pattern repeatedly.
Jesus looked at fishermen and saw apostles.
He looked at a tax collector and saw an evangelist.
He looked at a persecutor and saw a church planter.
He looked at sinners and saw redeemed sons and daughters.
The kingdom of God specializes in rewriting identities.
This is why Gideon's story matters.
Because many people reading this are still standing inside their own winepresses.
You may not be hiding from Midianites.
You may be hiding from failure.
You may be hiding from shame.
You may be hiding from regret.
You may be hiding from what others think.
You may even be hiding from God's calling because it feels too large and you feel too small.
"My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my family."
Grace reminds us that God's strength is not dependent upon our adequacy.
The Apostle Paul would later write in Greek:
ἡ γὰρ δύναμίς μου ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται
"hē gar dynamis mou en astheneia teleitai"
"For My power is made perfect in weakness."
The kingdom has always worked this way.
God chooses unlikely people so His glory becomes unmistakable.
Not because Gideon instantly became fearless.
Everything changed because God's presence entered the hiding place.
That is where transformation always begins.
The Gospel reaches its highest expression in Jesus Christ.
Humanity hid in the garden after sin entered the world.
The entire story of redemption is God pursuing hiding people.
Ultimately that pursuit led to a cross.
At Calvary, Jesus carried every shame, every failure, every fear, every hidden wound.
Three days later He rose again, proving that grace is stronger than sin, stronger than death, stronger than every hiding place we build.
This is why Gideon's story still speaks today.
Because before there was victory, there was fear.
Before there was courage, there was hiding.
Before there was transformation, there was grace.
And before there was a mighty warrior, there was a man standing in a winepress wondering whether God had forgotten him.
Maybe that is where you are today.
But perhaps the God who found Gideon is standing beside your winepress as well.
Perhaps He sees something in you that fear has blinded you from seeing.
Perhaps His grace is already rewriting the story.
Because that is what Jesus does.
He takes failures and creates testimonies.
He takes brokenness and creates beauty.
He takes scandals and creates redemption.
He takes hiding people and calls them into purpose.
What has been your winepress season?
What fear has God been calling you out of?
Because sometimes the greatest tragedy is not that we are hiding.
It is believing God cannot find us there.
